title: Short Trail Running Race: Beyond the Classic Model for Endurance Running Performance
authors: Ehrstrom S, Tartaruga MP, Easthope CS, Brisswalter J, Morin JB, Vercruyssen F
population: Nine highly trained trail runners performing a 27 km trail race plus laboratory tests
findings: VO2max, %VO2max at ventilatory threshold and level running economy gave a low prediction of the 27 km trail race time (R = 0.48).
A knee-extension fatigue index (local endurance, r = 0.91) and VO2max (r = -0.76) had the highest correlations with trail time.
Adding the fatigue index and running economy on a +10% slope markedly improved the model (R = 0.98); the fatigue index and VO2max had the largest unique contributions (49.8% and 20.4%).
The authors conclude the classic endurance model does not allow meaningful prediction of short trail performance.
limitations: n = 9 with several candidate predictors, so R = 0.98 is probably overfitted and unvalidated; 27 km only; homogeneous highly trained group; predictors are lab measures not available from a training log.
implications: Do not transfer a road-derived VDOT or CS directly to trail races; discount confidence and widen the range when the course is hilly.
Prefer course gradient data and the athlete's uphill performance over level-running metrics; do not code the R = 0.98 model.

verification.notes: Crossref gives short title 'Short Trail Running Race'; subtitle from Europe PMC. Corrected the researcher's 'elite-level males' (the abstract says highly trained, sex not stated) and clarified the fatigue index is a knee-extension local-endurance test.
